function.name: bash
function.description:
Executes a given bash command in a persistent shell session with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Be aware: OS: linux, Shell: bash

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

Use `/tmp/opencode` for temporary work outside the workspace. This directory has already been created, already exists, and is pre-approved for external directory access.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - Set `background: true` for long-running commands, or when other independent work can proceed in parallel. The tool returns immediately; you will be notified when the command finishes. Do not sleep or poll.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.
    - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)
  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.
    <good-example>
    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /foo/bar && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

# Committing changes with git

Once the user authorizes a coding task, you may create completion-supporting commits in its current worktree without asking separately. When creating a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may destroy work. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- Do not treat task authority as permission to commit unrelated changes

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel:
  - Run `git status` to see all untracked files. Never use the -uall flag.
  - Run `git diff` to see both staged and unstaged changes.
  - Run `git log --oneline -10` to see recent commit messages, so you can match the repo's commit style.
2. Analyze all staged changes and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (new feature, enhancement, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.)
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they request it.
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
3. Run the following commands:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- You may push the current non-protected task branch without separate confirmation when doing so supports the authorized task
- Landing on a protected branch, force-pushing, deploying, or modifying unrelated shared state still requires explicit authority
- Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported
- Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands
- If there are no changes to commit, do not create an empty commit
- ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC for correct formatting:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a GitHub URL, use the gh command to get the information needed.

When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel:
   - Run `git status` to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run `git diff` to see both staged and unstaged changes
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote
   - Run `git log` and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the branch
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the PR, looking at ALL commits (not just the latest):
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a GitHub PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

workdir.description: The working directory to run the command in. Defaults to the current directory. Use this instead of 'cd' commands.

background.description: Run the command in the background and return immediately. You will be notified when it finishes. Use for long-running commands or when other independent work can proceed in parallel. DO NOT sleep, poll, or wait for it.

function.name: ChangeDirectory
function.description: Change the active working directory for this session. Use this for persistent directory changes and for entering an existing Git worktree; a shell `cd` command affects only one shell invocation. Switching into a directory of another project requires approval.

directory.description: Directory to make active for this session. Relative paths resolve from the current working directory.

function.name: compact
function.description:
Compact the conversation at a natural checkpoint. Earlier history is replaced by a dense prefix plus the handoff note you write; the recent working set is preserved verbatim.
When to call it: at or above 100,000 context tokens, at the first natural checkpoint you reach. Below that, only when the user asks.
The test — imagine this conversation with the files you read and the large tool outputs stripped out. Your own words, your reasoning, and a list of the actions you took are what remain. If you could carry the work forward from that plus a short handoff note, compact now. If you would be stuck without re-reading, do not compact: keep working until your findings have become conclusions rather than raw material.
Natural checkpoints — compact here:
- The user made a decision or approved a plan, and the next steps are clear.
- You delivered a conclusion, analysis, or recommendation and the user has responded to it.
- Work landed: commit, push, deploy, merge, or PR complete.
- You are switching subsystems or approaches, or moving from investigation to implementation.
- Focused tests and typecheck pass on the change under test.
- A todo list is drained and the next batch is not yet defined.
- A long research or reading phase has been synthesized for the user.
- You are waiting on a long background job and the resume condition is one sentence.
Not checkpoints — keep working:
- Mid-investigation: a hypothesis is open, a bug is unexplained, the user just asked "why?" or said they do not understand.
- Mid-operation: between an edit and its verification, between a tool call and its result, or inside a test / build / commit sequence.
- The goal is still being negotiated and cannot be stated in two sentences.
- Only because a reminder appeared, or only because a lot has been read without synthesis.
Compacting at a checkpoint you choose is strictly better than the automatic compaction at the force boundary: you pick where the cut falls, and your handoff note is preserved.
Compaction treatment:
| Content | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Latest two user or visible assistant statements and intervening non-compaction parts | Preserved verbatim |
| Older user and assistant messages | Retained in a dense serialized prefix |
| Older reasoning/thoughts | Retained in the dense serialized prefix |
| Older tool calls | Signatures retained |
| Older tool outputs | Read, web-fetch/search, code-search, and large results are removed; selected short outputs may survive |
What you must provide:
- `handoff`: one multiline handoff note using the exact structure below.
- State the goal and intended completed state in one or two sentences.
- List concrete next steps, including verification or completion work.
- File-reference lines are optional. Include only files that may help recover missing or precise details, using one `<file>: <reason>` line per file. The successor should consult them as needed, not read them all by default.
Required structure:
# How to Reach the Goal and Which Files to Read

## <Short goal title>

<One or two sentences describing the goal and intended completed state.>

How to reach the goal:
- <Concrete next step>
- <Concrete next step>
- <Verification or completion step>

Consult these files as needed for missing or precise details; do not read them all by default:
<file>: <Why this file may be useful> (repeat as needed; omit file lines when none are useful)

Unrelated example:

# How to Reach the Goal and Which Files to Read

## Fix the login redirect bug

Ensure users return to their originally requested page after signing in without permitting unsafe external redirects. Add focused coverage for valid, missing, and malicious redirect values.

How to reach the goal:
- Trace how the requested URL moves from the authentication middleware to the login handler.
- Accept only validated local paths as redirect targets.
- Add tests for successful redirects and rejected external URLs.
- Run the focused authentication test suite.

Consult these files as needed for missing or precise details; do not read them all by default:
src/auth/middleware.ts: Defines how unauthenticated requests capture the original destination.
src/auth/login.ts: Selects and validates the redirect target after successful authentication.
src/auth/redirect.ts: Contains the local-path validation rules.
test/auth/redirect.test.ts: Covers expected redirect behavior and unsafe inputs.

function.name: continue_work
function.description:
Set the persistent continual-work mode for this Session.

Continual work combines a mode-specific continue-or-stop discipline with a
persisted north_star direction. Select an active mode proactively when the
work requires multiple phases, repeated verification, asynchronous operations,
or sustained investigation. Avoid it for a direct answer or a single
straightforward operation. When meaningful long-horizon work remains and you
are unsure, prefer the appropriate continual-work mode.

Once an active mode has been selected, it persists across provider turns,
ordinary user interactions, mode-prompt recurrence, mode switches, and
compaction. A successful call with mode "disabled" turns it off. As a safety
bound, the runtime also disables a mode after three consecutive mode-prompt
cycles repeat the same activity. The optional north_star argument is ignored
for disabled:

continue_work({ mode: "disabled" })

The first active-mode call requires north_star. Subsequent calls (including
mode switches) carry over the existing north_star automatically; supply a new
value only when the overall direction of the work has changed.

north_star is a concise direction for the work — roughly 500 characters
describing what you are trying to achieve, key constraints, and what done
looks like. It is a direction, not a log, plan, or status report. Use files,
todos, and the codebase itself to track progress and intermediate state.
Update north_star only when the direction changes, not to record progress.

Select the mode that describes the work currently required:

- planning: developing, correcting, reviewing, or validating a plan, specification, architecture, interface, or implementation design.

- feature: implementing and integrating requested behavior inside the current worktree, including completion-supporting tests, realistic verification, documentation, and work revealed during implementation.

- debugging: confirming that an observed failure is the reported problem, investigating its surrounding execution path, repairing it, adding a failing regression test where practical, verifying the user-visible workflow beyond unit tests, and inspecting for related regressions.

- testing: designing, strengthening, and executing evidence that software satisfies its contracts, including risk analysis, oracle selection, adversarial and property-based cases, deterministic checks, fault challenges, integration paths, and regression assessment.

- optimization: improving measured software runtime performance, memory use, or efficiency, including CUDA, kernel, compiler, and machine-learning systems optimization. Begin with the simplest credible approach. Add complexity only when measurement supports it, then simplify once the components responsible for improvement are understood.

- experimentation: designing, launching, debugging, monitoring, repairing, interpreting, and iterating on experiments, training runs, evaluations, benchmarks, and hyperparameter searches.

- disabled: the longer work period is complete, or further progress genuinely
  requires new authority or a critical user decision that reasonable
  investigation and best judgment cannot resolve.

Continue-work is for a new stage of progress. A monitor is for waiting on
an unchanged condition. If the next turn would only repeat the same
observation and reach the same conclusion, disable continue-work and start
a monitor. When the condition changes — finished, failed, stalled, or
otherwise newly actionable — stop the monitor and re-enter continue-work.
Do not spend the runtime's three-identical-cycle safety bound on passive
polling; hand the wait to a monitor after the first unchanged observation.
Do not re-enter continue-work just to look again. Re-entering to repeat
the last check means you should have been on a monitor. Stay in
continue-work while each turn can still change the work: implement,
launch, repair, interpret new evidence, write the report. Do not leave
because the next step is unspecified or because something is still in
progress.

When the user is clearly in discussion — questions, review, or
conversation rather than delegated work — explicitly disable continual work.
If a mode keeps recurring without progress, disable it. Ordinary user
interaction does not end an active work period automatically; after handling
the user's message, continue the authorized work unless you explicitly select
disabled.

At a continuation boundary, determine whether the user's orders, intent, and
applicable specification are complete; whether relevant work remains; and
whether reasonable next steps exist. Do not stop merely because the next step
was not specified in advance. Continue when further work reasonably
contributes to fulfilling the request.

The specification is not a standalone checklist and does not authorize
unrelated expansion. Its literal items can be complete while testing,
integration, discovered defects, documentation consistency, realistic
verification, or other mode-specific completion work remains.

Uncertainty is normally a reason to investigate, not to stop. Use code,
documentation, logs, tests, focused diagnostics, small experiments, prior
results, and repository history. Perfect certainty is unnecessary. Gather
enough evidence for a well-considered judgment.

If several choices remain equally good or nearly on par and their differences
are not critical, choose using best judgment and technical taste, then
continue. Ask the user only when reasonable investigation cannot reduce the
uncertainty enough for judgment and the unresolved choice changes materially
different user-valued outcomes, commits scarce GPU resources,
difficult-to-reverse shared state, an externally visible action, or another
expensive consequence.

Correctness uncertainty normally requires investigation and testing. Ask the
user when the unresolved issue is an intentional tradeoff among materially
different outcomes, such as competing definitions of correctness or
correctness versus quality, performance, compatibility, or cost.

Use this tool whenever the kind of work currently required changes or the
north_star direction needs a material update. Every successful active-mode
selection resets the runtime's mode-reassessment schedule. Work may evolve
between modes as evidence appears, but every transition must remain related to
the user's query and authorized intent. Examples include feature work entering
debugging after a failure, debugging returning to feature work after repair,
or experimentation entering debugging after an invalid run. These are
examples, not an exhaustive transition table; use judgment for similar
situations.

Do not cross scope merely because another kind of work is possible. Planning
or analysis does not authorize implementation by itself. Feature work does
not automatically authorize broad optimization. Debugging does not justify
an architectural rewrite before the reported problem and surrounding path
have been understood. Explicit user limits remain controlling.

**Parallel work may be substantial and bold.** Do user work while longer
operations run. Start long-running operations asynchronously when meaningful
independent work can continue. Parallel work must remain related to the
request, respect existing authority, avoid invalidating the active operation,
and avoid improperly competing for the GPU or other resource it requires.

mode.description: Registered continual-work mode to select, or disabled. See the tool description for available modes.

north_star.description: Concise direction for the work (~500 characters). Required for the first active-mode call; carried over automatically on subsequent calls. Ignored for disabled.

function.name: edit
function.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files. 

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file. 
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + colon + space (e.g., `1: `). Everything after that space is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the oldString or newString.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `oldString` is not found in the file with an error "oldString not found in content".
- The edit will FAIL if `oldString` is found multiple times in the file with an error "Found multiple matches for oldString. Provide more surrounding lines in oldString to identify the correct match." Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replaceAll` to change every instance of `oldString`. 
- Use `replaceAll` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

filePath.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

newString.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from oldString)

replaceAll.description: Replace all occurrences of oldString (default false)

function.name: EnterWorktree
function.description: Create or resume an isolated Git worktree and move this conversation into it. Reuse the current checkout when it is already a suitable dedicated worktree rather than creating another. The conversation and session ID remain unchanged.

name.description: Optional worktree name. When omitted, a name is generated.

function.name: ExitWorktree
function.description: Leave the current session worktree, either keeping it for later use or removing it. This only affects a worktree owned by this session.

action.description: Whether to keep the worktree for later use or remove it.

discard_changes.description: When removing, also discard uncommitted changes and commits.

function.name: glob
function.description:
- Fast file pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size
- Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts"
- Returns matching file paths
- Use this tool when you need to find files by name patterns
- When you are doing an open-ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Task tool instead
- You have the capability to call multiple tools in a single response. It is always better to speculatively perform multiple searches as a batch that are potentially useful.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

function.name: grep
function.description:
- Fast content search tool that works with any codebase size
- Searches file contents using regular expressions
- Supports full regex syntax (eg. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+", etc.)
- Filter files by pattern with the include parameter (eg. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}")
- Returns file paths and line numbers with matching lines
- Use this tool when you need to find files containing specific patterns
- If you need to identify/count the number of matches within files, use the Bash tool with `rg` (ripgrep) directly. Do NOT use `grep`.
- When you are doing an open-ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Task tool instead

pattern.description: The regex pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: The directory to search in. Defaults to the current working directory.

include.description: File pattern to include in the search (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}")

function.name: monitor
function.description: Schedule periodic prompts for yourself in this session. Each interval creates a visible synthetic user message with the configured prompt. If the session is busy, the message waits until current work settles. Starting again replaces the existing monitor; stop it when monitoring is no longer needed. The default prompt is "This is a monitor ping. Check your status."

interval_seconds.description: Seconds between monitor pings (minimum 10). Required when action is "start".

prompt.description: Synthetic user message to send on each interval. Defaults to "This is a monitor ping. Check your status."

function.name: read
function.description:
Read a file or directory from the local filesystem. If the path does not exist, an error is returned.

Usage:
- The filePath parameter should be an absolute path.
- By default, this tool returns up to 2000 lines from the start of the file.
- The offset parameter is the line number to start from (1-indexed).
- To read later sections, call this tool again with a larger offset.
- Use the grep tool to find specific content in large files or files with long lines.
- If you are unsure of the correct file path, use the glob tool to look up filenames by glob pattern.
- Contents are returned with each line prefixed by its line number as `<line>: <content>`. For example, if a file has contents "foo\n", you will receive "1: foo\n". For directories, entries are returned one per line (without line numbers) with a trailing `/` for subdirectories.
- Any line longer than 2000 characters is truncated.
- Call this tool in parallel when you know there are multiple files you want to read.
- Avoid tiny repeated slices (30 line chunks). If you need more context, read a larger window.
- This tool can read image files and PDFs and return them as file attachments.

filePath.description: The absolute path to the file or directory to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: The maximum number of lines to read (defaults to 2000)

function.name: skill
function.description:
Load a specialized skill when the task at hand matches one of the skills listed in the system prompt.

Use this tool to inject the skill's instructions and resources into current conversation. The output may contain detailed workflow guidance as well as references to scripts, files, etc in the same directory as the skill.

The skill name must match one of the skills listed in your system prompt.

name.description: The name of the skill from available_skills

function.name: task
function.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multistep tasks autonomously.

When using the Task tool, you must specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use.

When NOT to use the Task tool:
- If you want to read a specific file path, use the Read or Glob tool instead of the Task tool, to find the match more quickly
- If you are searching for a specific class definition like "class Foo", use the Grep tool instead, to find the match more quickly
- If you are searching for code within a specific file or set of 2-3 files, use the Read tool instead of the Task tool, to find the match more quickly
- If no available agent is a good fit for the task, use other tools directly


Usage notes:
1. Launch multiple agents concurrently whenever possible, to maximize performance; to do that, use a single message with multiple tool uses
2. Once you have delegated work to an agent, do not duplicate that work yourself. Continue with non-overlapping tasks, or wait for the result. For background tasks, you will be notified automatically when the result is ready.
3. When the agent is done, it will return a single message back to you. The result returned by the agent is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result. The output includes a task_id you can reuse later to continue the same subagent session.
4. Each agent invocation starts with a fresh context unless you provide task_id to resume the same subagent session (which continues with its previous messages and tool outputs). When starting fresh, your prompt should contain a highly detailed task description for the agent to perform autonomously and you should specify exactly what information the agent should return back to you in its final and only message to you.
5. The agent's outputs should generally be trusted
6. Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since it is not aware of the user's intent. Tell it how to verify its work if possible (e.g., relevant test commands).
7. If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first. Use your judgement.

Available agent types and the tools they have access to:
- explore: Fast agent specialized for exploring codebases. Use this when you need to quickly find files by patterns (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), search code for keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer questions about the codebase (eg. "how do API endpoints work?"). When calling this agent, specify the desired thoroughness level: "quick" for basic searches, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" for comprehensive analysis across multiple locations and naming conventions.
- general: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions and executing multi-step tasks. Use this agent to execute multiple units of work in parallel.

description.description: A short (3-5 words) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

task_id.description: This should only be set if you mean to resume a previous task (you can pass a prior task_id and the task will continue the same subagent session as before instead of creating a fresh one)

command.description: The command that triggered this task

function.name: todowrite
function.description:
Create and maintain a structured task list for the current coding session. Tracks progress, organizes multi-step work, and surfaces status to the user.

## When to use
Use proactively when:
- The task requires 3+ distinct steps or actions (not just 3 tool calls for a single conceptual step)
- The work is non-trivial and benefits from planning
- The user provides multiple tasks (numbered or comma-separated) or explicitly asks for a todo list
- New instructions arrive - capture them as todos
- You start a task - mark it `in_progress` (only one at a time) before working
- You finish a task - mark it `completed` and add any follow-ups discovered during the work

## When NOT to use
Skip when:
- The work is a single, straightforward task (or <3 trivial steps)
- The request is purely informational or conversational
- Tracking adds no organizational value

## States
- `pending` - not started
- `in_progress` - actively working (exactly ONE at a time)
- `completed` - finished successfully
- `cancelled` - no longer needed

## Rules
- Update status in real time; don't batch completions
- Mark `completed` only after the required work is actually done, including any required verification. Never based on intent.
- Keep exactly one `in_progress` while work remains
- If blocked or partial, keep it `in_progress` and add a follow-up todo describing the blocker
- Preserve user-provided commands verbatim (flags, args, order)
- Items should be specific and actionable; break large work into smaller steps

## Examples

Use it:
- "Add a dark mode toggle and run the tests" -> multi-step feature + explicit verification
- "Rename getCwd -> getCurrentWorkingDirectory across the repo" -> grep reveals 15 occurrences in 8 files
- "Implement registration, catalog, cart, checkout" -> multiple complex features

Skip it:
- "How do I print Hello World in Python?" -> informational
- "Add a comment to calculateTotal" -> single edit
- "Run npm install and tell me what happened" -> one command

When in doubt, use it.

status.description: Current status of the task: pending, in_progress, completed, cancelled

priority.description: Priority level of the task: high, medium, low

function.name: write
function.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
